The valuation on Nvidia ( NVDA ) is too appetizing for CEO Jensen Huang to ignore any longer. The king of AI chips revealed a stunning new $150 billion stock buyback plan on Monday — the largest share repurchase authorization increase in history. It brings the company's total buyback authorization to $235 billion. "NVIDIA's growth is being driven by a once-in-a-generation platform shift to AI and accelerated computing," Huang said in a statement. "Our cash generation gives us the capacity to invest in the technologies that advance this transformation and return capital to shareholders. This authorization reflects our confidence in the long-term opportunity ahead." Read more: What Nvidia's $150 billion stock buyback means for shareholders and potential investors Huang likely sees a great moment to buy back Nvidia shares on the cheap, ahead of further acceleration in AI development. Nvidia's forward price-to-earnings (P/E) multiple has declined steadily since August 2024, when artificial intelligence began to take hold, unleashing a boom in the company's stock price and earnings growth. The decline has only accelerated this year despite a series of strong quarters. The forward P/E ratio for Nvidia currently stands at 24 times, not too far removed from the S&P 500's ( ^GSPC ) 20-times multiple, despite the company being one of the fastest-growing companies in corporate America. Huang sees the disconnect. item.title: GoFundMe that raised nearly $290,000 for Texas couple pulled over 'factual' issues
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Donald and Josephine Johnson's GoFundMe campaign aimed to raise money for Josephine's cancer treatment. (KXAS) GoFundMe pulled the plug Sunday on a campaign to raise money for an elderly Texas couple, saying it had “identified factual misrepresentations.” The account was created after the husband went viral for working a backbreaking job to cover his wife’s mounting bills for cancer treatment. The digital fundraising site did not immediately reveal what kind of misrepresentations were behind its decision to end the campaign set to benefit Donald and Josephine Johnson. The GoFundMe gained national attention and raised nearly $290,000 before it was pulled down. The campaign was started by a “concerned stranger” identified as “Erin H,” who said she spotted on her Ring camera the 81-year-old husband struggling to carry heavy luggage up a flight of stairs. The organizer said she asked why he was working such a physically demanding job at his age, and Johnson said his wife was fighting cancer and this was the only job he could find to pay the overwhelming hospital bills. Door camera video shows Donald Johnson preparing to carry luggage up a flight of stairs. (KXAS) But somewhere along the line, GoFundMe said it found “misrepresentations” in the campaign. The platform received a tip that the organizer of the campaign might not be who they said they were. GoFundMe investigators called the organizer, who admitted that she was in fact the Johnsons’ daughter, that she had shot the viral video and that the concerned stranger was a made-up persona. The organizer, however, said the other aspects of Donald and Josephine Johnson’s story were true. She told GoFundMe’s team that the story would be more compelling if it were told by a stranger and not a family member. “Our Trust & Safety team identified factual misrepresentations, which directly violates our Terms of Service,” the platform said in a statement to NBC News on Sunday. “As a result, the fundraiser has been removed and all donors have been refunded.” The platform, which did not name the organizer of the fundraiser, said it has no choice but to take tough action in order to maintain trust with donors. “Ensuring GoFundMe is a safe and trusted place to give and receive help is our top priority. Taking action like this allows GoFundMe to protect donors’ generosity and our continued ability to support people who are fundraising to help others,” GoFundMe said. “GoFundMe’s policies, along with those of our payment processors, require authenticity and transparency for donors, and are strictly enforced,” it said. “Because that standard wasn’t met here, donors were protected under our GoFundMe Giving Guarantee , which guarantees a full refund in the rare case something isn’t right.” The Johnsons’ appeal for help has since been taken to an alternate fundraising site, GiveSendGo. There, the couple’s daughter, Amy Johnson, explained that her parents are fighting their mother’s pancreatic cancer and that the luggage-hauling job is real. “My dad is 81 and still works delivering luggage so they can stay afloat,” according to the GiveSendGo listing . “The neighbor story is real. The doorcam video is real. The diagnosis is real. The job is real.” A fundraising effort was already on for her dad via GoFundMe, but once the viral video emerged, the family decided to change the campaign’s organizer’s name to “Erin H,” to reflect the video captured by this stranger who wanted to remain anonymous, Amy Johnson said. But that name change amounted to an unintentional violation of GoFundMe terms, according to the daughter. “That was it. We didn’t know it was a problem,” the daughter said in a TikTok video . “I have to come out because someone wanted to do something out of pure kindness but wanted to remain anonymous.” Amy Johnson did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Donald Johnson could not immediately be reached. GiveSendGo calls itself a faith-based platform that hopes to “share God’s love” in the most efficient manner possible . It has been used to raise funds for Kenosha, Wisconsin, shooter Kyle Rittenhouse and a Minnesota woman caught using a racist slur on camera and to support Canadian truckers who blocked highways in protest of Covid restrictions . Asked about the validity of the Johnson campaign, GiveSendGo said in a statement: “We do not allow fundraisers to deceive the public about who or what is being fundraised for. Every fundraiser on GiveSendGo is reviewed by our verification team before any funds are released.” This article was originally published on NBCNews.com This article originally appeared on NBC News at https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/gofundme-texas-man-went-viral-hauling-bags-wifes-cancer-bills-removed-rcna600248

item.title: Education Department formally rescinds Title IX protections for LGBTQ students
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The Education Department announced Monday it has formally rescinded the Biden-era Title IX interpretation that gave sex-based discrimination protections to students on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity. Schools now must go back to the Title IX code as held under the previous Trump administration in 2020, which the department says will protect women’s sports. “Thanks to today’s action, the published Title IX regulations faithfully reflect court orders and Congressional intent — reducing confusion for parents, students, and educational institutions. We will continue to relentlessly champion equal opportunity for all Americans and hold accountable any school or college that violates the rights, privacy, or athletic opportunities of our women and girls,” Education Secretary Linda McMahon said. The Biden-era Title IX rule was already struck down in the court system after challenges from Republican states. And the administration has pursued its own definition since President Trump returned to office, making deals with schools such as the University of Pennsylvania to take transgender athletes out of their women’s programs. Opponents of the move say it will harm transgender athletes and weaken protections for sexual assault victims. “Sexual harassment and assault continue to be pervasive in schools and, to the fullest extent possible, we should be working to enforce the laws that protect student survivors of sexual violence. Yet, Education Secretary Linda McMahon and the Trump administration have decided to ignore what survivors need, instead weaponizing Title IX to attack trans students,” said Shiwali Patel, senior director of education justice at the National Women’s Law Center.
